extracted.intended_audience: patent lawyers, judges, and law students studying assignment/license and renewal/extension issues
extracted.subtask_description: Rules and principles governing what rights assignees, grantees, purchasers, and licensees acquire (or do not acquire) in relation to renewals, extensions, reissues, and subsequent patents; how instruments should be construed to determine whether future or extended terms are conveyed. Focuses on statutory Section 18 (act of 1836) and related case law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 18 protection for purchasers of patented machines
rubrics_metrics.description: A purchaser of a patented machine from a lawful source may use the identical machine as long as it lasts and may repair it after an extension of the patent; the sale carries the machine out of the monopoly and makes it the purchaser's property.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited cases: Chaffee v. Boston Belting Co., Bloomer v. Millingen, Farrington v. Board of Water Commissioners, Hawley v. Mitchell, Tilghman v. Mitchell. Explanation emphasizes that purchasers who derived a lawful right to use during the original term may continue to use and repair the machine after any extension. The doctrine is grounded on section 18 of the act of 1836 and on construing sale as taking the specific machine out of the monopoly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between right to make/vend and right to use after extension
rubrics_metrics.description: Mere assignees of the right to make and vend (franchise-like rights) who acquired under a former term generally take nothing under an extension unless there is an express stipulation, whereas purchasers/grantees of the right to use the patented article may continue to use it to the extent of their interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a controlling distinction in the cases: the right to make and vend is part of the franchise and ceases on extension absent stipulation; the right to use (especially of a sold machine) is treated as property of the purchaser and survives. Applicable when construing assignments and licenses made during original term.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumption that licenses/assignments relate to the existing term only
rubrics_metrics.description: In the absence of express provision indicating otherwise, instruments (licenses, assignments, covenants) are presumed to relate only to the patent term existing when the instrument was made and not to any subsequently obtained extension.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts will construe the whole instrument; common clauses like 'for and during the term for which said letters-patent are or may be granted' have often been held to refer only to reissues or the existing term, not to extensions, unless other language shows intent to include extensions. See cases discussed (e.g., Wilson v. Rousseau; Clum v. Brewer; Pitts v. Hall).

rubrics_metrics.name: Inchoate personal right to obtain statutory extension belongs to inventor
rubrics_metrics.description: The right to obtain an extension under the standing law (act of 1836) is an inchoate right intended as a reward to the inventor and belongs solely to the inventor or his personal representatives, not necessarily passing by a mere sale of the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the statutory extension was meant to compensate an inventor who received inadequate remuneration during the first term, courts construe conveyances narrowly so assignees do not receive the inchoate extension right absent clear expression of such intent. See Clum v. Brewer and related discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: A sale of the 'invention' does not automatically convey right to extended term
rubrics_metrics.description: A sale of the invention (during or before the original term) does not necessarily carry the exclusive right to an extended term obtained under the standing law; whether it does depends on the instrument showing an intent to convey beyond the first term.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court applies policy-based strict construction against transferring the inchoate extension right unless the contract language indicates such intent. Look to whole instrument for clauses pointing to duration and extent of the interest conveyed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Future contingent/potential extension interest can be conveyed but requires clear expression
rubrics_metrics.description: A future contingent interest in a patent (e.g., the possibility of an extension or subsequent patents) is capable of being a subject of bargain and sale, but its conveyance depends on whether the instrument manifests an intention to convey that contingent interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts examine the instrument's language and context to determine intent; broad language referring to 'all right, title and interest ... which may be secured ...' has been held to include reissues, renewals, and extensions in some cases (see Railroad Co. v. Trimble).

rubrics_metrics.name: Different legal effect of reissue (surrender and reissue) versus statutory extension
rubrics_metrics.description: A reissued patent (surrender and reissue to correct defects) is treated in law as the same patent and generally follows the interest of an assignee of the original; an extension obtained by statute or special act may be treated differently and not pass automatically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because a reissued patent is deemed to cover the same term and objects, phrases like 'may be granted' can sometimes be read to include reissues. By contrast, extensions (new additional term obtained by statute or special act) are subject to stricter construction and may not pass without clear language. See discussion around Wilson v. Rousseau and subsequent cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction of 'renewal' depends on the law in force and parties' presumed expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: When parties covenant regarding 'renewal' or 'renewed letters-patent,' the term is to be interpreted with reference to the rights and privileges provided by the patent system in existence at the time the covenant was made (e.g., likely referring to extensions under section 18 if that act was in force).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The courts presume parties meant what the law provided as a 'renewal' at that time. Subsequent legislation may fix the meaning, but interpretation rests on contemporaneous legal regime and reasonable expectation of the parties (see Wilson v. Rousseau; Pitts v. Hall).

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope-of-use questions for non-machine and mixed patents
rubrics_metrics.description: Applying the machine-focused decisions about sale and right-to-use to patents of other kinds (processes, mixed patents where machinery and process interplay) raises difficulties; whether the clause saving assignees' rights applies to these patents must be resolved case-by-case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: patented manufacture/process (e.g., patent starch) where patent covers right to make, use, and vend — questions arise what 'the right to use the thing patented' means and what 'extent of his interest therein' covers. Cases like Day v. Union India-Rub. Co. and Wilson v. Rousseau recognize the need for broader analysis when apparatus/process are blended.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whether grantee is confined to using the identical apparatus after extension is undecided
rubrics_metrics.description: It remains an open question whether an assignee or licensee of the right to use is confined, after an extension, to the use of the identical machine/apparatus in existence at the time of extension, or may use reconstructed/modified apparatus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supreme Court decisions to date involve use of machines constructed before the extension; they draw fine distinctions between permissible repairs (not changing identity) and reconstructions (which may change identity). Some lower-court decisions (e.g., Day v. Union India-Rub. Co., Wilson v. Simpson) permit broader rights in certain mixed cases. Courts must inquire into identity of machine, repairs versus reconstructions, and whether basis of construction (sale made it property) suffices in non-machine cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretive principle: prefer constructions avoiding unjust public consequences and aligning with legislative intent
rubrics_metrics.description: When choosing between two interpretations of ambiguous or involved statutory phraseology, courts should prefer the construction that most nearly accords with the legislature's intention and that avoids results fraught with unmixed evil or injustice (e.g., preventing sudden arrest of common use upon patent renewal).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text cites policy considerations (protection of individuals who purchased rights and avoidance of unjust consequences when patents are renewed) and holds that courts should assess practical effects upon the system in selecting among plausible interpretations. This principle governs statutory and contractual construction in this area.

rubrics_metrics.name: Phrases that commonly indicate inclusion of extensions versus those that do not
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain phraseologies have been held by courts to evidence an intent to include subsequent reissues/renewals/extensions (broad clauses like 'all the right, title, and interest ... which may be secured ... and to be held ... to the full end of the term for which said letters-patent are or may be granted'), whereas other formulations (e.g., 'for and during the term for which said letters-patent are or may be granted') have been interpreted as limited to reissues/existing term and not extending to statutory extensions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare cases: Phelps v. Comstock and Case v. Redfield (language held to include extension) vs. Hudson River & Harlem R.R. Co. (language held not to indicate extension). Courts examine exact wording and context; presence of explicit reference to 'extensions' or broad 'all patents ... whenever issued' language supports inclusion.
